newsitem.title: USA: Clinton to propose mark-to-market housing plan.
newsitem.headline: Clinton to propose mark-to-market housing plan.

text.p: The Clinton Administration on Wednesday is scheduled to unveil a bill to overhaul the Section 8 multifamily housing assistance program, according to a draft outline of the plan circulated by the administration on Tuesday.

"In an era of shrinking governmental resources, we cannot afford to continue to subsidize projects with rents in excess of market rents," the draft said in an introduction to a key section of the bill that would require many project owners to adjust inflated rents to market levels, or "mark-to-market."

The upcoming bill, which administration officials are scheduled to outline at an 1145 EDT press briefing on Wednesday, will be closely watched by muni market participants because many section 8 housing developers have financed their projects with tax-exempt bonds.
A key part of the bill includes tax incentives designed to get project owners to restructure their financings to permit them to charge market level rents rather than more inflated rents.

"Its very important," said one housing industry expert. Without the tax incentives, "the owners will do everything they can to avoid tax consequences, so they will delay, postpone and object to restructuring," the expert said.

Under the bill, owners could amortize taxes that they owe as a result of restructuring over a period up to 10 years, the draft says. They also would have incentives to sell projects to nonprofit groups under the bill.

Also, in exchange for favorable tax treatment, owners would agree to maintain 40 percent of the project's units at rents affordable to families that earn 60 percent of median income or less, the draft says.
The Federal Housing Administration would write off or forgive additional debt, to reflect the reduced income from those units, the draft says.

Owners whose mortgages have been reduced by more than 30 percent and less than 75 percent of the unpaid balance, could defer taxes from restructuring until the year in which their section 8 contract would have ended, the draft says.

The tax bill could then be amortized over 10 years, the draft says. Owners who sell to nonprofits in connection with restructuring could amortize the capital gains tax that results from sale over a seven-year period, the draft says.
The bill also would authorize a "range of tools" to restructure a project, including complete or partial write-off of the FHA-insured loan, the draft says.

Rents on restructured projects could not exceed fair market rents. Nonrestructured projects would be renewed at their current rents, not to exceed 120 percent of the fair market rent unless they meet three criteria.
Rents could exceed 120 percent of fair market rent if the project's primary financing or mortgage insurance is provided by a state government and the mortgage is not insured by FHA, the draft says.

Also, projects for the elderly (Section 202) and in rural areas could be rented at the higher level. And projects eligible for market-to-market that would not be "financially viable" at market rents, even with a complete write-off of the FHA-insured debt, could have a higher rent, the draft says.
